status_summary: Executive Order 14159 (2025-01-20) directed State and DHS to use INA 243(d) sanctions to the fullest extent of the law. The main visible measures found are entry proclamations under INA 212(f) and 215(a) rather than a formally cited 243(d) action: Proclamation 10949 (effective 2025-06-09) and Proclamation 10998 (effective 2026-01-01) fully suspend entry for 19 countries and partially suspend immigrant, B, F, M and J visas for 20 more, citing in part overstay rates and, for five countries, refusal to take back removable nationals. State made a B-1/B-2 visa bond program permanent on 2026-08-03, and a final rule published 2026-03-11 (effective 2026-04-10, starting with DV-2027) requires Diversity Visa entrants to submit valid passport information to curb fraud; a news report says State guidance of December 2025 also pauses issuance of all diversity visas. The design differs from the Mandate, which proposed country-specific 243(d) visa sanctions rather than broad entry bans, and the proclamations go beyond it in scope. On 2026-08-21 the Southern District of New York (Catholic Legal Immigration Network v. Rubio, No. 26-cv-00858-JAV, Judge Vargas) vacated a separate State policy, announced 2026-01-14 and in effect from 2026-01-21, pausing immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries on public-charge grounds, holding that it exceeded the Secretary's statutory authority and violated the INA's nondiscrimination provision; the opinion does not address Proclamation 10998 or INA 243(d), news summaries say the ruling did not affect Proclamation 10998, and a law-firm blog reports that State told the court on 2026-08-28 that the 75-country pause is no longer in effect. A secondary news report says State applied INA 243(d) in February 2026 to deny visas to eight Cuban baseball officials; that report cites no government source.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159, section 13, directed the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to implement the sanctions authorized by INA 243(d) to the fullest extent allowed, to build acceptance of removable nationals into diplomatic negotiations, and to weigh a country's delays in verifying identities (published 2025-01-29).

Proclamation 10949 suspended entry for nationals of 12 countries and partially for 7 (immigrant visas plus B, F, M and J), effective 2025-06-09, citing among other things overstay rates and refusal to accept removable nationals (published 2025-06-10).
State published a temporary rule creating a visa bond pilot program for B-1/B-2 applicants from designated countries; the pilot ran from 2025-08-20 to 2026-08-05.

Proclamation 10998 expanded the restrictions effective 2026-01-01: 19 countries fully suspended and 20 partially suspended (by this tracker's count), plus holders of Palestinian Authority travel documents, and removed the broad family-member exception (published 2025-12-19).

A secondary immigration-news report says State used INA 243(d) to deny visas to eight senior Cuban baseball officials, citing Cuba's refusal of regular deportation flights (month-level date, first of month used; not confirmed from a State or DHS source).

State publishes a final rule (91 FR 11891, effective 2026-04-10, starting with DV-2027) requiring Diversity Visa entrants to provide valid passport information and a scan of the passport page, to confirm identities earlier, support vetting and curb fraudulent third-party entries.

State's final rule made the visa bond program permanent for B-1/B-2 applicants from State-designated countries, with bonds of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000; country selection turns on overstay rates, information sharing and vetting weaknesses, and the rule does not list refusal to accept deportees as a criterion.

The Southern District of New York (Judge Jeannette Vargas, Catholic Legal Immigration Network v. Rubio, No. 26-cv-00858-JAV) grants plaintiffs partial summary judgment and vacates State's pause on immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries (announced 2026-01-14, effective 2026-01-21, implemented by a cable directing refusals under INA 221(g) on public-charge grounds). The court holds the policy contrary to law and beyond the Secretary's authority, including under the INA's nationality nondiscrimination provision, rejects a remand-only remedy, and does not address Proclamation 10998 or INA 243(d); news summaries say Proclamation 10998 was not affected.

title: Enforce visa reciprocity and INA 243(d) sanctions and review sensitive visa programs
uncertainties: I did not find or verify any actual invocation of INA 243(d); my search quota ran out before I could look for visa revocations or sanctions on specific countries (for example over deportee acceptance), reciprocity-schedule changes, student-visa vetting changes, or the Diversity Visa program pause. The Diversity Visa rule was identified by title only. The 19 and 20 country counts are my tally from the proclamation text (Turkmenistan counted among the partial group). The proclamation text lists Laos and Sierra Leone as moved from partial to full. Court challenges to the proclamations were not researched. The 243(d) use for Cuban officials and the 75-country pause start date (2026-01-21) come from a secondary immigration-news site and law-firm summaries; the S.D.N.Y. opinion was read (hosted by the National Immigration Law Center) and shows the pause was announced 2026-01-14 and effective 2026-01-21, on public-charge grounds, with no mention of INA 243(d) or Proclamation 10998. State's 2026-08-28 court filing was not located; the report that the pause ended rests on a law-firm blog. No State or DHS document applying INA 243(d) was found in the fetches of this pass (the Federal Register record of EO 14159 section 13 is the only primary document on 243(d)).
